stops.name: Rome — Cicero elected augur, the lituus taken up
stops.campa: Publius Crassus, son of the triumvir, falls with his father's army at Carrhae, and the college of augurs, sixteen priests who read the will of the gods in the flight and cry of birds, elects Cicero to the empty seat, an honor he says he had wanted above every other Roman distinction. He is given the curved staff, the lituus, with which the augur marks out the templum in the sky before he watches it, and he will carry that word's own root, aug-, increase, into a private meditation on why the office is called what it is.
stops.quote: The name augury is thought by the common people to come from the chattering of birds, but more rightly from augendo — that is, from the increase of the commonwealth.
stops.quote_source: Cicero, De Divinatione II.36, in the rendering carried by the Colegio Invisible essay 'Augury'

stops.name: Tusculum — De Re Publica finished, the Dream of Scipio
stops.campa: Before he must leave for his province, Cicero completes De Re Publica at Tusculum and closes it with the vision he gives to the younger Scipio Aemilianus: the elder Africanus comes to him in a dream and carries him up among the circling spheres, where the music made by their motion, too vast for mortal ears to catch waking, sounds without ceasing. Looking down, Scipio sees the whole earth shrunk to a point, the Roman empire itself no more than a pale mark upon it, and understands that the soul which serves the commonwealth well has a seat prepared for it beyond that turning light.
stops.quote: Iam ipsa terra ita mihi parva visa est, ut me imperii nostri, quo quasi punctum eius attingimus, paeniteret — And the earth itself seemed to me so small that I was ashamed of our empire, which, as it were, touches only a point of its surface.
stops.quote_source: Cicero, De Re Publica VI.16 (Somnium Scipionis)

stops.name: Tarsus, Cilicia — the reluctant proconsul arrives
stops.campa: Under Pompey's new law requiring a gap of years between office and province, Cicero, past fifty and wanting nothing less than to leave Rome and his books, is sent out as proconsul to govern Cilicia, a rough frontier province menaced by Parthia across the Amanus range. He sets up his tribunal at Tarsus and governs, by his own strict account, without taking a single gift, hearing cases himself rather than farming them to freedmen, and writing home constantly to Atticus that he counts the days until his year is done.

stops.name: Mount Amanus — hailed imperator
stops.campa: Cicero leads his legions against bandit strongholds in the Amanus range that divides Cilicia from Syria, storming several fortified villages by night assault and routing the free Cilician tribesmen who had never paid tribute to Rome. His soldiers salute him imperator on the field, an honor that in Rome carries the right to petition for a triumph, and for a season the philosopher-consul, more at ease with a stylus than a sword, finds himself, not without some pride he confesses to Atticus, a general in earnest.

stops.name: Pindenissum — the forty-seven day siege
stops.campa: Cicero brings his army against Pindenissum, the strongest fortress of the free Cilicians, said to trust so wholly in its cliffs that no army had ever taken it. He rings it with palisade and ditch, raises earthworks, mantlets, and a great siege tower, and batters it for forty-seven days through the start of winter until the defenders surrender on the Saturnalia. He sells the captives at auction to pay his troops, and writes to Atticus with the plain satisfaction of a man who has done, competently and completely, a piece of work he never wanted.
stops.quote: Cinximus vallo et fossa; aggere maximo, vineis, turre altissima, magna tormentorum copia, multis sagittariis, magno labore, apparatu, multis sauciis nostris, incolumi exercitu negotium confecimus — We ringed it with rampart and ditch; with a great earthwork, mantlets, a very tall tower, a large supply of engines and many archers, with much labour and equipment, with many of our men wounded but the army intact, we finished the business.

stops.name: Dyrrachium — crossing from Caieta to Pompey's camp
stops.campa: Caesar crosses the Rubicon and civil war breaks the uneasy peace Cicero has spent a decade trying to hold together. He hesitates for months, sick with divided loyalty to two men he has praised and feared in turn, before at last taking ship from Caieta on the seventh of June and crossing to Dyrrachium, to Pompey and the Senate's exiled government in the field. He brings no real gift for war and knows it; Pompey's officers mock his caustic jokes at their expense even as they rely on his name to give their cause the color of legitimacy it badly needs.

stops.name: Dyrrachium — Pharsalus, the battle he does not fight
stops.campa: Too unwell and too disillusioned to take the field, Cicero stays behind at Dyrrachium while Caesar destroys Pompey's army on the plain of Pharsalus in a single August afternoon. Pompey flees toward Egypt and his death; at the remnant camp Cato and the surviving nobles offer Cicero, as the ranking consular present, command of what is left of the republican cause. He refuses outright, certain now that further war only multiplies the ruin, and turns for home instead, earning Cato's open contempt and his own lasting reputation among the die-hard optimates as the man who quit at the harder half of the fight.

stops.name: Brundisium — Caesar's pardon
stops.campa: Cicero waits out a wretched year at Brundisium, uncertain whether the victorious dictator will treat him as a spared enemy or a dead man walking, until Caesar himself lands there returning from the East. Caesar, seeing the old consular waiting on the road, dismounts, embraces him, and walks with him alone a long way, talking of nothing but ordinary things, before either man mentions the war. It is pardon given as courtesy rather than as favor asked, and Cicero returns to Rome under it, stripped of command but alive, to a public life now conducted entirely at another man's pleasure.

stops.name: Tusculum — the death of Tullia
stops.campa: A month after bearing a son, Tullia, Cicero's daughter and by far the dearest person in his life, dies at Tusculum. Cicero collapses under a grief his friends have never seen in him and cannot recognize; he abandons Rome, abandons Terentia, whom he divorces within the year, and withdraws first to Atticus's house and then to his own villa at Astura on the shore, alone, walking the wooded island in the little river there for hours, unable to bear the sight of any other face. He begins reading every Greek consolation ever written on the death of a child, and finds none of them sufficient.
stops.quote: In hac solitudine careo omnium conloquio, cumque mane me in silvam abstrusi densam et asperam, non exeo inde ante vesperum — In this solitude I speak with no one, and when in the morning I have hidden myself away in a thick and rugged wood, I do not come out of it before evening.
stops.quote_source: Cicero, Letters to Atticus XII.15, written from Astura

stops.name: Tusculum — the dialogues of grief and old age
stops.campa: Out of the worst year of his life Cicero drives himself back to work at Tusculum, writing at a pace that astonishes even Atticus: the Tusculan Disputations on facing death and pain, On the Nature of the Gods, On Old Age for his friend Atticus, On Friendship in memory of the Scipio he never knew, all composed within months of one another. He turns Greek philosophy's whole vocabulary into workable Latin as he goes, inventing words the language did not have, so that Rome, exiled from politics under a dictator, might at least possess a philosophy of its own to suffer with.

stops.name: Rome, the Curia of Pompey — the Ides of March
stops.campa: Cicero sits among the senators in the hall built onto Pompey's theatre, called that day to a meeting of the Senate, and watches Caesar, dictator for life, go down under twenty-three blows from men he had pardoned. He had no part in the plot and learns of it only as it happens, but Brutus, lifting his bloody dagger clear of the body, is said to call out Cicero's name before any other, hailing the recovery of the republic's liberty in the one voice in Rome that liberty most needs. Cicero will spend what is left of his own life trying to make that shout true.

stops.name: Rome, the Temple of Concord — the First Philippic
stops.campa: Six months after the Ides, with Antony ruling Rome by decree and Caesar's assassins scattered or besieged, Cicero returns to the Senate meeting in the Temple of Concord and delivers the first of what he will come to call, in homage to Demosthenes against Philip of Macedon, his own Philippics. It is measured still, more warning than attack, but it announces to Antony and to Rome both that the old consular voice, silent through most of the dictatorship, has decided to speak again in its own name, whatever the cost of speaking proves to be.
